claim: Depriving immortalized mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) of all amino acids resulted in an initial loss of mTORC1 activity, as measured by the phosphorylation of its substrate, S6 kinase 1 (S6K1).
source: In agreement with previous reports, depriving immortalized mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) of all amino acids resulted in an initial loss of mTORC1 activity, as measured by the phosphorylation of its substrate, S6 kinase 1 (S6K1), yet a prolonged period of amino acid deprivation resulted in a near-complete reactivation of mTORC1 (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 1A showing phospho-S6K1 levels, and by citation to previous reports.

claim: A prolonged period of amino acid deprivation resulted in a near-complete reactivation of mTORC1.
source: In agreement with previous reports, depriving immortalized mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) of all amino acids resulted in an initial loss of mTORC1 activity, as measured by the phosphorylation of its substrate, S6 kinase 1 (S6K1), yet a prolonged period of amino acid deprivation resulted in a near-complete reactivation of mTORC1 (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 1A showing recovery of phospho-S6K1 levels over time.

claim: Reactivation of mTORC1 during prolonged amino acid deprivation was suppressed by bafilomycin A1, an inhibitor of lysosomal H+-ATPase.
source: Consistent with the pivotal role of the lysosome as a supplier of amino acids in conditions when extracellular amino acids are depleted, reactivation of mTORC1 was suppressed by bafilomycin A1, an inhibitor of lysosomal H+-ATPase.
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 1A showing that bafilomycin A1 treatment prevents mTORC1 reactivation.

claim: The lysosome plays a pivotal role as a supplier of amino acids in conditions when extracellular amino acids are depleted.
source: Consistent with the pivotal role of the lysosome as a supplier of amino acids in conditions when extracellular amino acids are depleted, reactivation of mTORC1 was suppressed by bafilomycin A1, an inhibitor of lysosomal H+-ATPase.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that inhibiting lysosomal function prevents mTORC1 reactivation, consistent with established knowledge about lysosomal amino acid supply.

claim: The onset of GCN2 activation in MEFs was gradual, with little autophosphorylation of Thr899 present at 1 hr post-amino acid withdrawal and then progressively increasing at subsequent time points.
source: In contrast to the rapid loss and subsequent recovery of mTORC1 activity following amino acid withdrawal, the onset of GCN2 activation in MEFs was gradual, with little autophosphorylation of Thr899 present at 1 hr post-amino acid withdrawal and then progressively increasing at subsequent time points (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 1A showing progressive increase in phospho-Thr899 GCN2 over time.

claim: The onset of GCN2 activation was mirrored by a gradual decline in the cellular translational output as reflected by the incorporation of O-propargyl-puromycin (OPP).
source: The onset of GCN2 activation was mirrored by a gradual decline in the cellular translational output as reflected by the incorporation of O-propargyl-puromycin (OPP), a tRNA-mimetic compound, into nascent polypeptides (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by OPP incorporation assay data in Figure 1B showing declining translation over time during amino acid deprivation.

claim: Even after 6 hr without extracellular amino acids, there remained ongoing translation in amino-acid-deprived cells in comparison to cells treated with the translation elongation inhibitor cycloheximide.
source: Importantly, even after 6 hr without extracellular amino acids, there remained ongoing translation in amino-acid-deprived cells in comparison to cells treated with the translation elongation inhibitor cycloheximide, demonstrating that amino-acid-deprived cells can continue to engage in adaptive translation even while bulk translation continues to decline.
evidence: Supported by OPP incorporation data in Figure 1B showing residual translation in amino acid-deprived cells compared to cycloheximide-treated cells.

claim: Amino-acid-deprived cells can continue to engage in adaptive translation even while bulk translation continues to decline.
source: Importantly, even after 6 hr without extracellular amino acids, there remained ongoing translation in amino-acid-deprived cells in comparison to cells treated with the translation elongation inhibitor cycloheximide, demonstrating that amino-acid-deprived cells can continue to engage in adaptive translation even while bulk translation continues to decline.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that translation continues at reduced levels during amino acid deprivation.

claim: ISRIB had only a minimal effect on the suppression of translation in amino-acid-deprived cells.
source: There was only a minimal effect of ISRIB on the suppression of translation in amino-acid-deprived cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) – even though it efficiently blocked ATF4 accumulation after 6 hr of amino acid deprivation and elicited a further increase in eIF2α phosphorylation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by OPP incorporation data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A showing minimal effect of ISRIB on translation.

claim: ISRIB efficiently blocked ATF4 accumulation after 6 hr of amino acid deprivation.
source: There was only a minimal effect of ISRIB on the suppression of translation in amino-acid-deprived cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) – even though it efficiently blocked ATF4 accumulation after 6 hr of amino acid deprivation and elicited a further increase in eIF2α phosphorylation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B showing reduced ATF4 levels with ISRIB treatment.

claim: ISRIB elicited a further increase in eIF2α phosphorylation during amino acid deprivation.
source: There was only a minimal effect of ISRIB on the suppression of translation in amino-acid-deprived cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) – even though it efficiently blocked ATF4 accumulation after 6 hr of amino acid deprivation and elicited a further increase in eIF2α phosphorylation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B showing increased phospho-eIF2α with ISRIB treatment.

claim: GCN2-mediated eIF2α phosphorylation was not the major cause of the suppression of translation associated with amino acid withdrawal.
source: This observation suggests that GCN2-mediated eIF2α phosphorylation was not the major cause of the suppression of translation associated with amino acid withdrawal.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ISRIB, which counteracts eIF2α phosphorylation effects, does not rescue translation suppression.

claim: tRNAGln charging was significantly reduced at 1 hr of amino acid deprivation (p<0.05).
source: In contrast, tRNAGln charging was significantly reduced at 1 hr (p<0.05) and was almost completely uncharged at 6 hr (p<0.001) (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by tRNA charging assay data in Figure 1C showing reduced tRNAGln charging at 1 hr.

claim: tRNAGln was almost completely uncharged at 6 hr of amino acid deprivation (p<0.001).
source: In contrast, tRNAGln charging was significantly reduced at 1 hr (p<0.05) and was almost completely uncharged at 6 hr (p<0.001) (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by tRNA charging assay data in Figure 1C showing near-complete loss of tRNAGln charging at 6 hr.

claim: The charging of amino acids on initiator tRNAMet, tRNALeu, tRNAArg, and tRNAVal was maintained not only after 1 hr, but even after 6 hr of amino acid deprivation.
source: The charging of amino acids on initiator tRNAMet, tRNALeu, tRNAArg, and tRNAVal was maintained not only after 1 hr, but even after 6 hr of amino acid deprivation (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by tRNA charging assay data in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D showing maintained charging of these tRNAs.

claim: Intracellular free glutamine levels declined more than other amino acids during amino acid deprivation.
source: Mass spectrometry analysis revealed that intracellular free glutamine levels declined more than other amino acids as well (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E showing greater decline in glutamine levels.

claim: Amino acid charging of methionine, arginine, and leucine tRNAs was maintained despite significant reductions in their intracellular free amino acid levels 1 hr after cells were placed in amino-acid-deficient medium.
source: Amino acid charging of methionine, arginine, and leucine tRNAs was maintained despite the fact that we measured significant reductions in their intracellular free amino acid levels 1 hr after cells were placed in amino-acid-deficient medium (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by tRNA charging data and mass spectrometry data in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: When cells were deprived of amino acids for 6 hr in the presence of bafilomycin A1 to impair lysosomal function, the charge on tRNAVal and initiator tRNAMet pools could no longer be maintained.
source: In support of this prediction, when cells were deprived of amino acids for 6 hr in the presence of bafilomycin A1 to impair lysosomal function, the charge on tRNAVal and initiator tRNAMet pools could no longer be maintained (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by tRNA charging assay data in Figure 1D showing loss of tRNAVal and tRNAMet charging with bafilomycin A1 treatment.

claim: Bafilomycin A1 treatment did not lead to a further increase in GCN2 phosphorylation at 6 hr of amino acid deprivation.
source: Notably, bafilomycin A1 treatment did not lead to a further increase in GCN2 phosphorylation, which may indicate that the amount of uncharged tRNAGln present in the cell at the 6 hr time point is sufficient to reach the upper limit of the tRNA-sensing capacity of GCN2.
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 1A showing no additional increase in GCN2 phosphorylation with bafilomycin A1.

claim: The amount of uncharged tRNAGln present in the cell at the 6 hr time point may be sufficient to reach the upper limit of the tRNA-sensing capacity of GCN2.
source: Notably, bafilomycin A1 treatment did not lead to a further increase in GCN2 phosphorylation, which may indicate that the amount of uncharged tRNAGln present in the cell at the 6 hr time point is sufficient to reach the upper limit of the tRNA-sensing capacity of GCN2.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the observation that GCN2 phosphorylation does not increase further with bafilomycin A1.

claim: Both cycloheximide and L-valinol promoted accumulation of the charged form of tRNAGln in amino-acid-deprived cells.
source: Indeed, both cycloheximide and L-valinol promoted accumulation of the charged form of tRNAGln (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: Supported by tRNA charging assay data in Figure 1E and 1F showing increased tRNAGln charging with these inhibitors.

claim: L-valinol resulted in the loss of charge on tRNAVal, which is consistent with its activity as a competitive inhibitor of valyl-tRNA synthetase.
source: In addition, L-valinol, but not cycloheximide, resulted in the loss of charge on tRNAVal, which is consistent with its activity as a competitive inhibitor of valyl-tRNA synthetase (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by tRNA charging assay data in Figure 1F showing loss of tRNAVal charging with L-valinol, consistent with known mechanism.

claim: The rapid accumulation of the charged form of tRNAGln upon translation inhibition indicates that the charged form of tRNAGln continues to be produced in amino-acid-deprived cells but is rapidly consumed in protein synthesis.
source: The rapid accumulation of the charged form of tRNAGln upon translation inhibition indicates that the charged form of tRNAGln continues to be produced in amino-acid-deprived cells but is rapidly consumed in protein synthesis, which is consistent with the observation that translation continues to take place in cells completely deprived of extracellular free amino acids (Figure 1B).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that translation inhibitors rapidly restore tRNAGln charging, indicating ongoing charging and consumption.

claim: Neither the synthesis of glutamine nor its recovery through protein degradation is sufficient to maintain tRNA charging in the absence of an extracellular supply of glutamine.
source: However, the results suggest that neither the synthesis of glutamine nor its recovery through protein degradation is sufficient to maintain tRNA charging in the absence of an extracellular supply of glutamine.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that tRNAGln becomes depleted despite ongoing protein degradation and potential glutamine synthesis.

claim: tRNAGln, but not tRNAVal or tRNAiMet became uncharged in cells that were deprived of amino acids for 6 hr, as confirmed by northern hybridization-based tRNA charging assay.
source: In agreement with the results obtained via the periodate-based assay, we found that tRNAGln, but not tRNAVal or tRNAiMet became uncharged in cells that were deprived of amino acids for 6 hr, whereas addition of L-valinol has partially recovered the charged form of tRNAGln.
evidence: Supported by northern blot data in Figure 1G showing selective uncharging of tRNAGln.

claim: Addition of L-valinol partially recovered the charged form of tRNAGln in amino-acid-deprived cells.
source: In agreement with the results obtained via the periodate-based assay, we found that tRNAGln, but not tRNAVal or tRNAiMet became uncharged in cells that were deprived of amino acids for 6 hr, whereas addition of L-valinol has partially recovered the charged form of tRNAGln.
evidence: Supported by northern blot data in Figure 1G showing recovery of tRNAGln charging with L-valinol.

claim: Culturing MEFs in a medium formulation in which each amino acid was supplied at the level of 5% of that in standard DMEM resulted in tRNAGln charging being almost completely lost (p=0.0011), while other tRNA isoacceptors remained charged.
source: To address this issue, we cultured MEFs in a medium formulation in which each amino acid was supplied at the level of 5% of that in standard DMEM. Even under these conditions where extracellular glutamine is at 200 μM, we found that tRNAGln charging was almost completely lost (p=0.0011), while other tRNA isoacceptors remained charged (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by tRNA charging assay data in Figure 1H showing selective loss of tRNAGln charging in 5% AA medium.

claim: The depletion of the charged form of tRNAGln in 5% AA medium was accompanied by an increase in GCN2 phosphorylation.
source: The depletion of the charged form of tRNAGln under these conditions was accompanied by an increase in GCN2 phosphorylation (Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 1I showing increased GCN2 phosphorylation in 5% AA medium.

claim: Amino acid deprivation in quiescent MEFs resulted in a similar pattern of GCN2 induction as in proliferating MEFs.
source: However, amino acid deprivation in quiescent MEFs resulted in a similar pattern of GCN2 induction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F) as well as in a selective loss of charged tRNAGln (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G), indicating that the inability of cells to maintain tRNAGln charge in amino-acid-deprived state was independent of the cell's proliferative status.
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F showing GCN2 activation in quiescent cells.

claim: Amino acid deprivation in quiescent MEFs resulted in a selective loss of charged tRNAGln.
source: However, amino acid deprivation in quiescent MEFs resulted in a similar pattern of GCN2 induction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F) as well as in a selective loss of charged tRNAGln (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G), indicating that the inability of cells to maintain tRNAGln charge in amino-acid-deprived state was independent of the cell's proliferative status.
evidence: Supported by tRNA charging assay data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G showing loss of tRNAGln charging in quiescent cells.

claim: The inability of cells to maintain tRNAGln charge in amino-acid-deprived state was independent of the cell's proliferative status.
source: However, amino acid deprivation in quiescent MEFs resulted in a similar pattern of GCN2 induction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F) as well as in a selective loss of charged tRNAGln (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G), indicating that the inability of cells to maintain tRNAGln charge in amino-acid-deprived state was independent of the cell's proliferative status.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that both proliferating and quiescent cells show similar tRNAGln depletion patterns.

claim: CHARGE-seq reliably detected 49 out of 50 known cytosolic tRNA isodecoders and determined their charge status.
source: This method allowed us to reliably detect 49 out of 50 known cytosolic tRNA isodecoders and determine their charge status (a tRNA for IleGAT returned a low number of reads and was excluded from the analysis).
evidence: Supported by CHARGE-seq methodology and results presented in Figure 2C.

claim: The two known tRNAGln isodecoders – those corresponding to glutamine codons CAG and CAA – were the sole class of cytosolic tRNAs that became uncharged in amino-acid-deprived cells.
source: The CHARGE-seq readout confirmed that tRNAGln becomes selectively uncharged in amino-acid-deprived cells. In fact, the assay revealed that the two known tRNAGln isodecoders – those corresponding to glutamine codons CAG and CAA – were the sole class of cytosolic tRNAs that became uncharged in amino-acid-deprived cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by CHARGE-seq data in Figure 2C showing selective uncharging of tRNAGln isodecoders.

claim: Glutaminase inhibitor CB-839 rescued the charge on both tRNAGln isodecoders in amino-acid-depleted cells, while having no discernible effect on tRNA charging in amino-acid-replete cells.
source: Furthermore, glutaminase inhibitor CB-839 rescued the charge on both tRNAGln isodecoders in amino-acid-depleted cells, while having no discernible effect on tRNA charging in amino-acid-replete cells.
evidence: Supported by CHARGE-seq data in Figure 2C showing restoration of tRNAGln charging with CB-839 in amino acid-depleted conditions.

claim: The rescue of charged tRNAGln by CB-839 was accompanied by the uncharging of initiator and elongator tRNAMet species, as well as a reduced charging of several other tRNAs.
source: Interestingly, we also found that the rescue of charged tRNAGln by CB-839 was accompanied by the uncharging of initiator and elongator tRNAMet species, as well as a reduced charging of several other tRNAs, which might indicate that tRNAMet is the second-most limiting tRNA class in MEFs subjected to amino acid deprivation.
evidence: Supported by CHARGE-seq data in Figure 2C showing changes in tRNAMet and other tRNA charging with CB-839.

claim: tRNAMet may be the second-most limiting tRNA class in MEFs subjected to amino acid deprivation.
source: Interestingly, we also found that the rescue of charged tRNAGln by CB-839 was accompanied by the uncharging of initiator and elongator tRNAMet species, as well as a reduced charging of several other tRNAs, which might indicate that tRNAMet is the second-most limiting tRNA class in MEFs subjected to amino acid deprivation.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the observation that tRNAMet becomes uncharged when tRNAGln is restored.

claim: GLS inhibition had only a marginal effect on GCN2 phosphorylation in MEFs deprived of amino acids for 6 hr.
source: Consistent with the observed CB-839-triggered depletion of charged tRNAMet, GLS inhibition had only a marginal effect on GCN2 phosphorylation in MEFs deprived of amino acids for 6 hr (Figure 2E), or when cells were cultured for 24 hr in a 5% amino acid DMEM formulation, in which each amino acid contained in standard DMEM was supplied at a fraction equaling 5% of that in DMEM (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 2E showing minimal change in GCN2 phosphorylation with CB-839.

claim: A498 and MiaPaCa2 cell lines show selective depletion of tRNAGln when deprived of extracellular amino acids that can be recovered by treatment with CB-839.
source: As presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, A498, a renal cell line, and MiaPaCa2, a pancreatic cell line, show selective depletion of tRNAGln when deprived of extracellular amino acids that can be recovered by treatment with CB-839 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by tRNA charging assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and 1B showing tRNAGln depletion and rescue with CB-839.

claim: In MiaPaCa2 cells, uncharging of tRNAArg was detected when tRNAGln charging was restored.
source: Instead, uncharging of tRNAArg was detected in MiaPaCa2 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), but not in A498 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by tRNA charging assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B showing tRNAArg uncharging in MiaPaCa2.

claim: The limiting nature of various charged tRNA pools may be dictated by the cellular context and differences in metabolism of individual amino acids in these cells.
source: These observations indicate that the limiting nature of various charged tRNA pools may be dictated by the cellular context and differences in metabolism of individual amino acids in these cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that different cell types show different patterns of compensatory tRNA uncharging.

claim: The specific loss of charged tRNAMet in amino-acid-deprived MEFs upon restoring the charged form of tRNAGln could be potentially explained by the critical role of methionine in S-adenosyl-methionine (SAM) production in support of cellular methylation and glutathione production through the transsulfuration pathway.
source: The specific loss of charged tRNAMet in amino-acid-deprived MEFs upon restoring the charged form of tRNAGln could be potentially explained by the critical role of methionine in S-adenosyl-methionine (SAM) production in support of cellular methylation and glutathione production through the transsulfuration pathway (Zhu et al., 2019).
evidence: Speculative explanation based on known metabolic roles of methionine, supported by citation.

claim: MiaPaCa2 is deficient for argininosuccinate synthetase (ASS1), and is, as a result, an arginine auxotroph.
source: This finding may indicate that arginine is more profoundly limiting in amino-acid-depleted MiaPaCa2 cells than even methionine. This effect could be explained by the fact that MiaPaCa2, as are many other PDAC-derived lines, is deficient for argininosuccinate synthetase (ASS1), and is, as a result, an arginine auxotroph (Singh et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Singh et al., 2019 describing ASS1 deficiency in MiaPaCa2.

claim: The inability of MiaPaCa2 cells to produce arginine de novo from citrulline and aspartate may explain why arginine becomes the most limiting substrate for tRNA charging when tRNAGln charging is restored.
source: The inability of MiaPaCa2 cells to produce arginine de novo from citrulline and aspartate may thus explain the observed phenomenon that as soon as tRNAGln charging is restored in these cells, arginine becomes the most limiting substrate for tRNA charging.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that tRNAArg becomes uncharged when tRNAGln is restored, combined with knowledge of MiaPaCa2's arginine auxotrophy.

claim: The rescue of tRNAGln charging by CB-839 in amino-acid-deprived A498 cells leads to a near-complete reversal of amino acid depletion-triggered GCN2 activation.
source: Of note, the observed lack of compensatory tRNA uncharging is mirrored by a near-complete reversal of amino acid depletion-triggered GCN2 activation in A498 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D) in contrast to MEFs (Figure 2E,F) and MiaPaCa2 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and 1D showing reversal of GCN2 activation with CB-839 in A498 cells.

claim: CB-839 inhibited proliferation of MEFs, A498, and MiaPaCa2 cells in complete (100% AA) medium.
source: In agreement with published studies, CB-839 inhibited proliferation of MEFs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G), A498 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H), and MiaPaCa2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I) cells in complete (100% AA) medium.
evidence: Supported by cell proliferation data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G-I, consistent with published studies.

claim: Cell lines were not sensitive to glutaminase inhibition when cultured in low AA DMEM (5% AA).
source: However, the cell lines were not sensitive to glutaminase inhibition when cultured in low AA DMEM (5% AA).
evidence: Supported by cell proliferation data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G-I showing no growth inhibition with CB-839 in 5% AA medium.

claim: CB-839 treatment enabled proliferation of A498 cells in 5% AA DMEM.
source: In fact, CB-839 treatment enabled proliferation of A498 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H) in 5% AA DMEM.
evidence: Supported by cell proliferation data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H showing increased proliferation with CB-839 in 5% AA medium.

claim: While glutaminase activity is beneficial for fueling biosynthesis and cell proliferation when amino acids are plentiful, it may become a liability for cells that encounter amino-acid-poor environments.
source: Collectively, these observations suggest that while glutaminase activity is beneficial for fueling biosynthesis and cell proliferation when amino acids are plentiful, it may, in fact, become a liability for cells that encounter amino-acid-poor environments.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that glutaminase inhibition is detrimental in nutrient-rich but beneficial in nutrient-poor conditions.

claim: Cells maintain a robust expression of glutaminase regardless of the status of their amino acid supply.
source: Indeed, we detected that cells maintain a robust expression of glutaminase regardless of the status of their amino acid supply (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J), further supporting the key role of glutaminase in depleting charged tRNAGln in amino-acid-poor conditions.
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1J showing consistent GLS expression across conditions.

claim: CB-839 treatment suppressed the eventual reactivation of mTORC1 upon a prolonged amino acid deprivation in all cell types tested.
source: CB-839 treatment also suppressed the eventual reactivation of mTORC1 upon a prolonged amino acid deprivation in all cell types tested (Figure 2E,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–F), while no effect of CB-839 on mTORC1 activity in presence of amino acids was evident.
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 2E, 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-F showing reduced mTORC1 reactivation with CB-839.

claim: By restoring charged tRNAGln pools, inhibition of glutaminolysis may bolster adaptive translation in amino-acid-depleted environments, which may deplete the levels of essential amino acids such as methionine and arginine needed to activate mTORC1.
source: One possible explanation of this effect is that by restoring charged tRNAGln pools, inhibition of glutaminolysis may, in fact, bolster adaptive translation in amino-acid-depleted environments. This increase in translation may deplete the levels of essential amino acids such as methionine (Figure 2D) and arginine (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), needed to activate mTORC1.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the observed suppression of mTORC1 reactivation by CB-839.

claim: CB-839 treatment was associated with an increase in ATF4 accumulation in amino-acid-poor conditions across all cellular contexts tested.
source: Intriguingly, CB-839 treatment was associated with an increase in ATF4 accumulation in amino-acid-poor conditions across all cellular contexts tested (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), despite eliciting no further increase in GCN2 phosphorylation.
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, 1F showing increased ATF4 with CB-839.

claim: ATF4 protein has a half-life of only 1 hr.
source: However, ATF4 protein is also a very short-lived protein with a half-life of only 1 hr (Lassot et al., 2001) – which, paradoxically, makes its accumulation highly dependent on the cellular ability to carry out translation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lassot et al., 2001 describing ATF4 half-life.

claim: The increase in ATF4 accumulation in amino-acid-depleted cells upon CB-839 treatment may indicate that restoring tRNAGln charging augments the total cellular capacity for translation.
source: Taking this into account, the increase in ATF4 accumulation in amino-acid-depleted cells upon CB-839 treatment may indicate that restoring tRNAGln charging augments the total cellular capacity for translation – which, in turn, allows cells to accumulate more ATF4.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ATF4, a short-lived protein, accumulates more with CB-839 treatment.

claim: Glutaminase inhibition markedly increased bulk translation in amino-acid-deprived cells.
source: Indeed, glutaminase inhibition markedly increased bulk translation in amino-acid-deprived cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by OPP incorporation data in Figure 3A showing increased translation with CB-839.

claim: A similar effect on translation was observed with other available GLS inhibitors – BPTES and Compound 968.
source: A similar effect was observed with other available GLS inhibitors – BPTES and Compound 968 (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by OPP incorporation data in Figure 3B showing increased translation with BPTES and Compound 968.

claim: Supplying L-glutamine at the concentration of 200 μM facilitated translation in amino-acid-deprived cells to an extent similar to that seen upon GLS inhibition.
source: Moreover, supplying L-glutamine at the concentration of 200 μM (which represents 5% of DMEM formulation) facilitated translation in amino-acid-deprived cells to an extent similar to that seen upon GLS inhibition (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by OPP incorporation data in Figure 3C showing increased translation with glutamine supplementation.

claim: Supplying 10 μM L-methionine had no effect on the overall translation rate in amino-acid-deprived cells.
source: In contrast, supplying 10 μM L-methionine (5% of DMEM formulation) had no effect on the overall translation rate, indicating that translation in amino-acid-deprived cells is hampered specifically by the deficit of charged tRNAGln, which must be resolved before any benefit could be derived from resupplying other limiting amino acids.
evidence: Supported by OPP incorporation data in Figure 3C showing no effect of methionine supplementation.

claim: Translation in amino-acid-deprived cells is hampered specifically by the deficit of charged tRNAGln, which must be resolved before any benefit could be derived from resupplying other limiting amino acids.
source: In contrast, supplying 10 μM L-methionine (5% of DMEM formulation) had no effect on the overall translation rate, indicating that translation in amino-acid-deprived cells is hampered specifically by the deficit of charged tRNAGln, which must be resolved before any benefit could be derived from resupplying other limiting amino acids.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that glutamine but not methionine supplementation rescues translation.

claim: Either glutaminase inhibition or supplementation of exogenous glutamine rescued amino acid withdrawal-associated suppression of translation in MiaPaCa2 and A498 cells.
source: Similarly to the effects observed in MEFs, either glutaminase inhibition or supplementation of exogenous glutamine rescued amino acid withdrawal-associated suppression of translation in MiaPaCa2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and A498 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) cells as well.
evidence: Supported by OPP incorporation data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and 1B showing translation rescue in these cell lines.

claim: The loss of tRNAGln charging is a key limiting factor for new protein synthesis in amino-acid-poor conditions across a variety of cellular contexts.
source: This result indicates that the loss of tRNAGln charging is a key limiting factor for new protein synthesis in amino-acid-poor conditions across a variety of cellular contexts.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that restoring tRNAGln charging rescues translation across multiple cell types.

claim: A 6 hr amino acid deprivation led to a precipitous decline in d2GFP signal, while having no effect on the stable GFP levels.
source: Indeed, a 6 hr amino acid deprivation led to a precipitous decline in d2GFP signal, while having no effect on the stable GFP levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by FACS data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C showing differential effects on GFP and d2GFP.

claim: The decline in d2GFP during amino acid deprivation could not be explained by an increase in clearance of d2GFP from amino-acid-deprived cells.
source: This effect could not be explained by an increase in clearance of d2GFP from amino-acid-deprived cells, as measured by a cycloheximide chase (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D showing no change in d2GFP clearance rate.

claim: Adding CB-839 or 5% L-Gln to amino-acid-deprived cells resulted in an increase in d2GFP accumulation.
source: Consistent with the observed effect on OPP incorporation, adding CB-839 or 5% L-Gln to amino-acid-deprived cells resulted in an increase in d2GFP accumulation (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by FACS data in Figure 3D showing increased d2GFP with CB-839 or glutamine.

claim: ISRIB had no effect on d2GFP accumulation in amino-acid-deprived cells.
source: No such effect was observed when amino-acid-deprived cells were treated with eIF2B activator ISRIB. This suggests that the effect of CB-839 on GFP accumulation is not a consequence of the relief of the phospho-eIF2α-driven translational inhibition.
evidence: Supported by FACS data in Figure 3D showing no effect of ISRIB on d2GFP.

claim: The effect of CB-839 on d2GFP accumulation is not a consequence of the relief of the phospho-eIF2α-driven translational inhibition.
source: No such effect was observed when amino-acid-deprived cells were treated with eIF2B activator ISRIB. This suggests that the effect of CB-839 on GFP accumulation is not a consequence of the relief of the phospho-eIF2α-driven translational inhibition.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ISRIB does not affect d2GFP accumulation.

claim: CB-839 treatment did not prevent the clearance of d2GFP from cells in which translation was arrested with cycloheximide.
source: Finally, CB-839 treatment did not prevent the clearance of d2GFP from cells in which translation was arrested with cycloheximide, suggesting that CB-839-driven increase in d2GFP was not due to a non-specific interference of CB-839 with the protein degradation machinery (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by FACS data in Figure 3D showing d2GFP clearance with cycloheximide regardless of CB-839.

claim: CB-839-driven increase in d2GFP was not due to a non-specific interference of CB-839 with the protein degradation machinery.
source: Finally, CB-839 treatment did not prevent the clearance of d2GFP from cells in which translation was arrested with cycloheximide, suggesting that CB-839-driven increase in d2GFP was not due to a non-specific interference of CB-839 with the protein degradation machinery (Figure 3D).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that CB-839 does not affect d2GFP clearance when translation is blocked.

claim: IgG yield by A20 cells was reduced when amino acids were limiting.
source: As expected, IgG yield by A20 cells was reduced when amino acids were limiting, yet a concomitant inhibition of glutaminase with CB-839 restored it to a level comparable to that seen in amino-acid-replete cells (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: Supported by dot blot data in Figure 3E and quantification in Figure 3F showing reduced IgG in low amino acid conditions.

claim: Inhibition of glutaminase with CB-839 restored IgG yield in amino-acid-limited A20 cells to a level comparable to that seen in amino-acid-replete cells.
source: As expected, IgG yield by A20 cells was reduced when amino acids were limiting, yet a concomitant inhibition of glutaminase with CB-839 restored it to a level comparable to that seen in amino-acid-replete cells (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: Supported by dot blot data in Figure 3E and quantification in Figure 3F showing IgG restoration with CB-839.

claim: The selective loss of charged tRNAGln limits translation in amino-acid-depleted cells, which can be counteracted by adding exogenous glutamine or blocking glutamine consumption in a glutaminolysis reaction.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the selective loss of charged tRNAGln limits translation in amino-acid-depleted cells, which can be counteracted by adding exogenous glutamine or blocking glutamine consumption in a glutaminolysis reaction.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing that glutamine supplementation or glutaminase inhibition rescues translation.

claim: There are 68 proteins in the human proteome that contain uninterrupted tracts of 10 or more glutamine residues, known as polyglutamine, or polyQ, tracts.
source: However, there are 68 proteins in the human proteome that contain uninterrupted tracts of 10 or more glutamine residues, known as polyglutamine, or polyQ, tracts.
evidence: Factual statement about the human proteome, likely based on established knowledge.

claim: PolyQ tracts are thought to provide flexibility within multisubunit protein complexes.
source: PolyQ tracts are thought to provide flexibility within multisubunit protein complexes (Tóth-Petróczy et al., 2008) as well as to be functionally involved in phase separation phenomena (Fiumara et al., 2010; Vitalis et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tóth-Petróczy et al., 2008.

claim: PolyQ tracts are functionally involved in phase separation phenomena.
source: PolyQ tracts are thought to provide flexibility within multisubunit protein complexes (Tóth-Petróczy et al., 2008) as well as to be functionally involved in phase separation phenomena (Fiumara et al., 2010; Vitalis et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fiumara et al., 2010 and Vitalis et al., 2007.

claim: Expansions of polyQ tracts in select proteins underlie the pathology of several neurodegenerative diseases including Huntington's disease and spinocerebellar ataxia.
source: In addition, expansions of polyQ tracts in select proteins underlie the pathology of a several neurodegenerative diseases including Huntington's disease and spinocerebellar ataxia (Lieberman et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lieberman et al., 2019.

claim: Culturing MiaPaCa2 cells in amino-acid-depleted conditions (5% AA) significantly reduced the levels of several polyQ proteins, including TATA-box binding protein (TBP), mediator complex subunit 12 (MED12), core binding factor α1 (CBPα1), and CREB-binding protein (CBP).
source: Indeed, culturing MiaPaCa2 cells in amino-acid-depleted conditions (5% AA) significantly reduced the levels of several polyQ proteins, including TATA-box binding protein (TBP), mediator complex subunit 12 (MED12), core binding factor α1 (CBPα1), and CREB-binding protein (CBP).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 4A showing reduced polyQ protein levels in 5% AA.

claim: Proteins lacking polyQ tracts showed little to no depletion in 5% AA, indicating that polyQ-containing proteins are particularly sensitive to amino acid deficit.
source: In contrast, proteins lacking polyQ tracts showed little to no depletion in 5% AA, indicating that polyQ-containing proteins are particularly sensitive to amino acid deficit (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 4A showing differential effects on polyQ vs non-polyQ proteins.

claim: Supplementing amino-acid-depleted medium with either CB-839 or glutamine restored the levels of all four polyQ-containing proteins tested.
source: Furthermore, supplementing amino-acid-depleted medium with either CB-839 or glutamine restored the levels of all four polyQ-containing proteins tested, suggesting that levels of polyQ proteins can be modulated by changes in the availability of glutamine for translation.
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 4A showing restoration of polyQ protein levels with CB-839 or glutamine.

claim: Levels of polyQ proteins can be modulated by changes in the availability of glutamine for translation.
source: Furthermore, supplementing amino-acid-depleted medium with either CB-839 or glutamine restored the levels of all four polyQ-containing proteins tested, suggesting that levels of polyQ proteins can be modulated by changes in the availability of glutamine for translation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that glutamine availability affects polyQ protein levels.

claim: Exposing cells to limiting amino acid conditions markedly suppressed incorporation of labeled uridine into nascent RNA.
source: Indeed, we found that exposing cells to limiting amino acid conditions markedly suppressed incorporation of labeled uridine into nascent RNA, which could be partially restored by CB-839 or added glutamine, thus mirroring the effect these conditions had on polyQ protein levels (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by 5-EU incorporation data in Figure 4B showing reduced RNA synthesis in amino acid-limited conditions.

claim: The suppression of RNA synthesis in amino acid-limited conditions could be partially restored by CB-839 or added glutamine.
source: Indeed, we found that exposing cells to limiting amino acid conditions markedly suppressed incorporation of labeled uridine into nascent RNA, which could be partially restored by CB-839 or added glutamine, thus mirroring the effect these conditions had on polyQ protein levels (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by 5-EU incorporation data in Figure 4B showing partial restoration of RNA synthesis with CB-839 or glutamine.

claim: shRNA constructs targeting human GLS resulted in a significant rescue of both polyQ protein expression and labeled uridine incorporation in amino-acid-depleted cells.
source: Similarly to the effects observed with CB-839 and with exogenous glutamine supplementation, shRNA constructs targeting human GLS, but not control shRNAs, resulted in a significant rescue of both polyQ protein expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) as well as of labeled uridine incorporation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E) in amino-acid-depleted cells.
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and 5-EU incorporation data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Glutaminase inhibition did not increase the size of nucleotide triphosphate pools in amino-acid-depleted cells.
source: Importantly, glutaminase inhibition did not increase the size of nucleotide triphosphate pools in amino-acid-depleted cells, indicating that its effect on RNA synthesis is unlikely to be explained by increased nucleotide availability under these conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F showing no increase in NTP pools with CB-839.

claim: The effect of glutaminase inhibition on RNA synthesis is unlikely to be explained by increased nucleotide availability.
source: Importantly, glutaminase inhibition did not increase the size of nucleotide triphosphate pools in amino-acid-depleted cells, indicating that its effect on RNA synthesis is unlikely to be explained by increased nucleotide availability under these conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that NTP pools do not increase with glutaminase inhibition.

claim: The presence of polyQ tracts within transcriptional regulators may represent an amino-acid-sensing adaptation that allows a cell to modulate transcriptional output in response to changes in amino acid availability.
source: Taken together, these observations raise the possibility that the presence of polyQ tracts within transcriptional regulators may represent an amino-acid-sensing adaptation that allows a cell to modulate transcriptional output in response to changes in amino acid availability.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the collective observations about polyQ proteins and transcription.

claim: Even though both glutamine-poor and leucine-poor conditions equivalently inhibited bulk translation, only glutamine-poor formulations led to a significant depletion of polyQ proteins.
source: Even though both glutamine-poor and leucine-poor conditions equivalently inhibited bulk translation, only glutamine-poor formulations led to a significant depletion of polyQ proteins (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by puromycin incorporation and western blot data in Figure 4C showing differential effects of glutamine vs leucine depletion.

claim: Depletion of glutamine specifically, and not the inhibition of translation associated with the depletion of a different amino acid, is responsible for the observed decline in polyQ protein levels.
source: Taken together, these observations indicate that depletion of glutamine specifically, and not the inhibition of translation associated with the depletion of a different amino acid, is responsible for the observed decline in polyQ protein levels.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that only glutamine depletion, not leucine depletion, affects polyQ protein levels.

claim: Recombinant TBP with an intact polyQ tract behaved similarly to endogenous TBP protein – its levels declined precipitously in amino-acid-depleted conditions and were fully restored by CB-839.
source: As expected, recombinant TBP with an intact polyQ tract behaved similarly to endogenous TBP protein – that is, its levels declined precipitously in amino-acid-depleted conditions and were fully restored by CB-839 (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 4D showing similar behavior of recombinant and endogenous TBP.

claim: Levels of recombinant TBP lacking the polyQ tract (ΔpolyQ TBP-HA) showed no decline upon amino acid depletion.
source: In contrast, levels of recombinant TBP lacking the polyQ tract (ΔpolyQ TBP-HA) showed no decline upon amino acid depletion.
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 4D showing stable levels of ΔpolyQ TBP-HA.

claim: The polyQ tract is required for the sensitivity of TBP to amino acid depletion.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that the polyQ tract is required for the sensitivity of TBP to amino acid depletion.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that removing the polyQ tract eliminates TBP's sensitivity to amino acid depletion.

claim: PolyQ-GFP-expressing cells accumulated markedly less fluorescence in amino-acid-depleted than in complete medium.
source: In contrast to control GFP-expressing cells, in which the amount of fluorescence accumulation over the course of 6 hr was not affected by the absence of extracellular amino acids, PolyQ-GFP-expressing cells accumulated markedly less fluorescence in amino-acid-depleted than in complete medium (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by FACS data in Figure 4F showing reduced PolyQ-GFP accumulation in amino acid-depleted conditions.

claim: The reduced PolyQ-GFP accumulation in amino-acid-deprived cells could not be attributed to the decreased half-life of PolyQ-GFP protein.
source: This effect could not be attributed to the decreased half-life of PolyQ-GFP protein in amino-acid-deprived cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G showing no change in PolyQ-GFP half-life.

claim: Both CB-839 and supplementing additional glutamine facilitated PolyQ-GFP accumulation in amino-acid-deprived cells.
source: Importantly, both CB-839 and supplementing additional glutamine facilitated PolyQ-GFP accumulation in amino-acid-deprived cells, providing additional evidence that restoring charged tRNAGln pools may ameliorate the defect in polyQ protein synthesis in an amino-acid-limited state (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by FACS data in Figure 4G showing increased PolyQ-GFP with CB-839 or glutamine.

claim: Restoring charged tRNAGln pools may ameliorate the defect in polyQ protein synthesis in an amino-acid-limited state.
source: Importantly, both CB-839 and supplementing additional glutamine facilitated PolyQ-GFP accumulation in amino-acid-deprived cells, providing additional evidence that restoring charged tRNAGln pools may ameliorate the defect in polyQ protein synthesis in an amino-acid-limited state (Figure 4G).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that treatments that restore tRNAGln charging improve polyQ protein synthesis.

claim: An RNAi-mediated depletion of tRNAGln, or an overexpression of tRNAAla, leads to a decreased translational fidelity of polyQ tracts in human huntingtin transcript, resulting in a −1 ribosomal frameshift.
source: A recent study of translation of polyglutamine-containing human huntingtin transcript has revealed that an RNAi-mediated depletion of tRNAGln, or an overexpression of tRNAAla, leads to a decreased translational fidelity of its polyQ tract, resulting in a −1 ribosomal frameshift from a (CAG)n into a (GCA)n frame, and consequently, formation of a polyalanine-containing polypeptide product (Girstmair et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Girstmair et al., 2013.

claim: While PolyQ−1-GFP-expressing MEFs cultured in complete medium expressed no GFP, amino acid deprivation triggered a marked GFP accumulation.
source: Indeed, while PolyQ−1-GFP-expressing MEFs cultured in complete medium expressed no GFP, amino acid deprivation triggered a marked GFP accumulation. This effect was completely blocked by CB-839 (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by FACS data in Figure 5B showing GFP accumulation in amino acid-deprived conditions.

claim: CB-839 completely blocked the amino acid deprivation-triggered GFP accumulation in PolyQ−1-GFP-expressing MEFs.
source: Indeed, while PolyQ−1-GFP-expressing MEFs cultured in complete medium expressed no GFP, amino acid deprivation triggered a marked GFP accumulation. This effect was completely blocked by CB-839 (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by FACS data in Figure 5B showing no GFP accumulation with CB-839 treatment.

claim: Growth of MiaPaCa2 cells in 5% AA medium triggered GFP accumulation in PolyQ−1-GFP-expressing cells.
source: To test whether human cells also exhibited a loss of translational fidelity, MiaPaCa2 cells were cultured in 5% AA DMEM for 24 hr. Growth in 5% AA medium triggered GFP accumulation as well (Figure 5C), and this accumulation was also suppressed by CB-839 (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) or by adding exogenous glutamine (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by FACS data in Figure 5C showing GFP accumulation in 5% AA medium.

claim: GFP accumulation in PolyQ−1-GFP-expressing MiaPaCa2 cells was suppressed by CB-839 or by adding exogenous glutamine.
source: To test whether human cells also exhibited a loss of translational fidelity, MiaPaCa2 cells were cultured in 5% AA DMEM for 24 hr. Growth in 5% AA medium triggered GFP accumulation as well (Figure 5C), and this accumulation was also suppressed by CB-839 (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) or by adding exogenous glutamine (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by FACS data in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A showing suppression of GFP with CB-839 or glutamine.

claim: No frameshift-dependent translation of GFP was observed in MiaPaCa2 cells grown in complete (100% AA) medium with or without CB-839.
source: In contrast, no frameshift-dependent translation of GFP was observed in MiaPaCa2 cells grown in complete (100% AA) medium with or without CB-839.
evidence: Supported by FACS data in Figure 5C showing no GFP in complete medium.

claim: A similar pattern of frameshift-dependent GFP expression was evident in PolyQ−1-GFP reporter-transduced murine colon carcinoma cell line MC38.
source: A similar pattern was also evident in PolyQ−1-GFP reporter-transduced murine colon carcinoma cell line MC38 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by FACS data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B showing similar pattern in MC38 cells.

claim: The extent of GFP accumulation in PolyQ−1-GFP reporter correlated with the extent of amino acid depletion.
source: Notably, the extent of GFP accumulation correlated with the extent of amino acid depletion. Thus, a milder (10%) amino acid depletion also resulted in GFP accumulation within 24 hr, albeit to a lesser extent than what was observed in 5% DMEM (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by FACS data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C showing dose-dependent GFP accumulation.

claim: ISRIB had no effect on the frameshift-dependent GFP expression in PolyQ−1-GFP reporter.
source: In contrast to glutamine pool-restoring treatments such as glutaminase inhibition and supplementing additional exogenous glutamine, amino acid stress response inhibitor ISRIB had no effect on the GFP expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that the frame shifting effect is unlikely to be orchestrated by eIF2α phosphorylation-associated amino acid stress response program.
evidence: Supported by FACS data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D showing no effect of ISRIB on GFP.

claim: The frame shifting effect is unlikely to be orchestrated by eIF2α phosphorylation-associated amino acid stress response program.
source: In contrast to glutamine pool-restoring treatments such as glutaminase inhibition and supplementing additional exogenous glutamine, amino acid stress response inhibitor ISRIB had no effect on the GFP expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that the frame shifting effect is unlikely to be orchestrated by eIF2α phosphorylation-associated amino acid stress response program.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ISRIB does not affect frameshift-dependent GFP expression.

claim: Across a variety of cellular contexts, amino acid depletion renders translation of polyglutamine-tract-containing transcripts prone to frame shifting.
source: Taken together, these observations indicate that across a variety of cellular contexts, amino acid depletion renders translation of polyglutamine-tract-containing transcripts prone to frame shifting.
evidence: Inferred from observations across multiple cell types showing frameshift-dependent GFP expression.

claim: Inhibiting glutaminase or supplying exogenous glutamine counters the loss of translational fidelity in the PolyQ−1-GFP reporter context.
source: In addition, we found that inhibiting glutaminase or supplying exogenous glutamine counters the loss of translational fidelity in this reporter context, which implicates the deficit of the charged form of tRNAGln in this phenomenon.
evidence: Supported by FACS data showing that CB-839 and glutamine suppress frameshift-dependent GFP expression.

claim: The deficit of the charged form of tRNAGln is implicated in the loss of translational fidelity on polyQ tracts.
source: In addition, we found that inhibiting glutaminase or supplying exogenous glutamine counters the loss of translational fidelity in this reporter context, which implicates the deficit of the charged form of tRNAGln in this phenomenon.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that restoring tRNAGln charging prevents frameshifting.

claim: Only amino acid depletion-associated stress resulted in GFP accumulation in PolyQ−1-GFP reporter, not other cellular stresses.
source: Only amino acid depletion-associated stress resulted in GFP accumulation, indicating that amino acid deficit is a specific trigger for translational frame shifting.
evidence: Supported by FACS data in Figure 5D showing GFP accumulation only with amino acid depletion.

claim: Amino acid deficit is a specific trigger for translational frame shifting on polyQ tracts.
source: Only amino acid depletion-associated stress resulted in GFP accumulation, indicating that amino acid deficit is a specific trigger for translational frame shifting.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that only amino acid depletion, not other stresses, triggers frameshifting.

claim: Luc−1-GFP cells displayed minimal GFP accumulation in amino-acid-depleted medium (5% AA).
source: In contrast to PolyQ−1-GFP reporter-expressing cells, Luc−1-GFP cells displayed minimal GFP accumulation in amino-acid-depleted medium (5% AA, Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by FACS data in Figure 5E showing minimal GFP in Luc−1-GFP cells.

claim: While PolyQ−1-GFP reporter-expressing cells accumulated significantly more GFP in glutamine-poor than in leucine-poor conditions, Luc−1-GFP cells accumulated only modest levels of GFP in either depleted medium formulation.
source: Furthermore, while PolyQ−1-GFP reporter-expressing cells accumulated significantly more GFP in glutamine-poor than in leucine-poor conditions, Luc−1-GFP cells accumulated only modest levels of GFP in either depleted medium formulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by FACS data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E showing differential responses of the two reporters.

claim: The presence of a polyQ tract promotes translational frame shifting in response to amino acid depletion.
source: Taken together, these observations indicate that the presence of a polyQ tract promotes translational frame shifting in response to amino acid depletion.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that PolyQ−1-GFP but not Luc−1-GFP shows significant frameshifting.

claim: PolyQ-associated frame shifting is triggered specifically by the depletion of glutamine rather than that of any given amino acid.
source: Taken together, these observations indicate that the presence of a polyQ tract promotes translational frame shifting in response to amino acid depletion. Furthermore, our findings indicate that polyQ-associated frame shifting is triggered specifically by the depletion of glutamine rather than that of any given amino acid.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that glutamine depletion has a greater effect on frameshifting than leucine depletion.

claim: The loss of translational fidelity triggered by amino acid depletion can be reversed by re-feeding the amino-acid-depleted cells with amino-acid-rich medium.
source: Indeed, when PolyQ−1-GFP-expressing MiaPaCa2 cells exposed to 5% AA DMEM for 24 hr were cultured in 100% AA DMEM for an additional 72 hr, GFP levels have declined markedly (Figure 5F), demonstrating that the frame shifting phenomenon is contingent upon amino acid deficit and is readily reversed once the adequate amino acid supply is restored.
evidence: Supported by FACS data in Figure 5F showing decline in GFP after re-feeding with complete medium.

claim: The frame shifting phenomenon is contingent upon amino acid deficit and is readily reversed once the adequate amino acid supply is restored.
source: Indeed, when PolyQ−1-GFP-expressing MiaPaCa2 cells exposed to 5% AA DMEM for 24 hr were cultured in 100% AA DMEM for an additional 72 hr, GFP levels have declined markedly (Figure 5F), demonstrating that the frame shifting phenomenon is contingent upon amino acid deficit and is readily reversed once the adequate amino acid supply is restored.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that GFP levels decline when cells are re-fed with complete medium.

claim: Translation of polyglutamine-tract-containing transcripts is prone to frame shifting in response to amino acid deficit but not to other types of cellular stresses in diverse cellular contexts.
source: Taken together, our observations indicate that in diverse cellular contexts, translation of polyglutamine-tract-containing transcripts is prone to frame shifting in response to amino acid deficit but not to other types of cellular stresses, and can be augmented by treatments that restore tRNAGln to its charged state.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing frameshift specificity to amino acid depletion across cell types.

claim: Frameshifting of polyQ tracts can be augmented by treatments that restore tRNAGln to its charged state.
source: Taken together, our observations indicate that in diverse cellular contexts, translation of polyglutamine-tract-containing transcripts is prone to frame shifting in response to amino acid deficit but not to other types of cellular stresses, and can be augmented by treatments that restore tRNAGln to its charged state.
evidence: Inferred from observations that CB-839 and glutamine supplementation reduce frameshifting.

claim: Multiple nests of ~10–100 GFP+ cells were observed residing within the PolyQ−1-GFP-transduced xenografts, while no staining was present in control xenografts.
source: The staining revealed multiple nests of ~10–100 GFP+ cells residing within the PolyQ−1-GFP-transduced xenografts, while no staining was present in control xenografts (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 6A showing GFP+ cell nests in xenografts.

claim: No GFP+ clones emerged when PolyQ−1-GFP-transduced MiaPaCa2 cells were seeded at clonal density in vitro (0 out of 6 10 cm dishes assayed).
source: To rule out the possibility that these nests might represent outgrowths of rare clones that are constitutively GFP-positive regardless of amino acid availability, we seeded PolyQ−1-GFP –transduced MiaPaCa2 cells at a clonal density in vitro. No GFP+ clones have emerged in this setting (0 out of 6 10 cm dishes assayed), indicating that groups of GFP+ cells observed in vivo are unlikely to be products of rare clonal outgrowths.
evidence: Supported by clonal density seeding experiment showing no constitutively GFP+ clones.

claim: Groups of GFP+ cells observed in vivo are unlikely to be products of rare clonal outgrowths.
source: To rule out the possibility that these nests might represent outgrowths of rare clones that are constitutively GFP-positive regardless of amino acid availability, we seeded PolyQ−1-GFP –transduced MiaPaCa2 cells at a clonal density in vitro. No GFP+ clones have emerged in this setting (0 out of 6 10 cm dishes assayed), indicating that groups of GFP+ cells observed in vivo are unlikely to be products of rare clonal outgrowths.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that no GFP+ clones emerge in vitro.

claim: The translational frame shifting of polyglutamine tracts can be observed in discrete areas within solid tumors in vivo.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that the translational frame shifting of polyglutamine tracts can be observed in discrete areas within solid tumors in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of GFP+ cell nests in xenografts.

claim: The proportion of GFP+ cells in xenografts was highest at week 3 and declined to a lower but reproducible level at week 5.
source: Interestingly, the proportion of GFP+ cells was highest at week 3 and declined to a lower but reproducible level at week 5 (Figure 6B), suggesting that either GFP+ cells are selected against over time or that cancer cells reduce their level of mistranslation as the xenografts mature.
evidence: Supported by FACS data in Figure 6B showing temporal changes in GFP+ cell proportion.

claim: Either GFP+ cells are selected against over time or cancer cells reduce their level of mistranslation as the xenografts mature.
source: Interestingly, the proportion of GFP+ cells was highest at week 3 and declined to a lower but reproducible level at week 5 (Figure 6B), suggesting that either GFP+ cells are selected against over time or that cancer cells reduce their level of mistranslation as the xenografts mature.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the temporal decline in GFP+ cells.

claim: Cells have the capacity to maintain pools of charged tRNAs during interruptions in extracellular amino acid supply.
source: The present work demonstrates that cells have the capacity to maintain pools of charged tRNAs during interruptions in extracellular amino acid supply.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing maintained tRNA charging for most amino acids during amino acid deprivation.

claim: The ability to maintain a charged tRNA compartment in amino-acid-deprived cells requires lysosomal function.
source: The ability to maintain a charged tRNA compartment in amino-acid-deprived cells requires lysosomal function, which is consistent with the established role of the lysosome as a critical source of amino acids in a nutrient-limited state.
evidence: Supported by data showing that bafilomycin A1 prevents maintenance of tRNA charging, consistent with known lysosomal function.

claim: Adaptive translation over time results in a selective depletion of tRNAGln charging that reduces the net translation.
source: Our work further reveals that adaptive translation over time results in a selective depletion of tRNAGln charging that reduces the net translation.
evidence: Inferred from observations showing progressive tRNAGln depletion and translation decline during amino acid deprivation.

claim: The reduction in translation during amino acid deprivation does not occur because cells cannot either recycle glutamine from lysosome-degraded proteins or take up sufficient extracellular glutamine when the vascular delivery of amino acids is compromised.
source: This reduction in translation does not occur because cells cannot either recycle glutamine from lysosome-degraded proteins or take up sufficient extracellular glutamine when the vascular delivery of amino acids is compromised.
evidence: Inferred from observations that tRNAGln continues to be charged but is rapidly consumed.

claim: The reduction in translation during amino acid deprivation results from the propensity of cells to convert glutamine to glutamate through glutaminase.
source: Instead, it results from the propensity of cells to convert glutamine to glutamate through glutaminase.
evidence: Inferred from observations that glutaminase inhibition restores tRNAGln charging and translation.

claim: Inhibiting glutaminase in the context of amino acid deficit augments the capacity of amino-acid-depleted cells to maintain tRNAGln charging and sustain protein synthesis.
source: Indeed, we found that inhibiting glutaminase in the context of amino acid deficit augments the capacity of amino-acid-depleted cells to maintain tRNAGln charging and sustain protein synthesis.
evidence: Supported by multiple experiments showing that glutaminase inhibition restores tRNAGln charging and translation.

claim: Even though glutaminase inhibition suppresses growth when amino acids are abundant, it facilitates translation and even cell proliferation when amino acid supply is limited.
source: This indicates that even though glutaminase inhibition suppresses growth when amino acids are abundant, it facilitates translation and even cell proliferation when amino acid supply is limited.
evidence: Supported by cell proliferation data showing differential effects of glutaminase inhibition in nutrient-rich vs nutrient-poor conditions.

claim: Amino acid limitation-associated depletion of tRNAGln results in a collective depletion of a number of key core transcription factors whose protein sequences contain polyglutamine tracts and consequently reduces cellular transcriptional output.
source: Amino acid limitation-associated depletion of tRNAGln also results in a collective depletion of a number of key core transcription factors whose protein sequences contain polyglutamine tracts and consequently reduces cellular transcriptional output.
evidence: Supported by western blot and 5-EU incorporation data showing reduced polyQ transcription factors and RNA synthesis.

claim: The position of a polyQ tract is not tethered to a fixed position within the primary protein sequence among orthologs from diverse taxa.
source: Interestingly, a comparative sequence analysis across a broad spectrum of metazoan proteomes has revealed multiple instances in which the position of a polyQ tract is not tethered to a fixed position within the primary protein sequence among orthologs from diverse taxa.
evidence: Supported by citation to Schaefer et al., 2012.

claim: The mere presence – rather than a specific location – of a polyQ tract may be of functional importance.
source: This observation suggests that the mere presence – rather than a specific location – of a polyQ tract may be of functional importance (Schaefer et al., 2012).
evidence: Inferred from comparative sequence analysis, supported by citation.

claim: Polyglutamine tracts in proteins may carry out a nutrient-sensing function by changing the protein level in response to extracellular amino acid availability.
source: Altogether, our observations raise the possibility that polyglutamine tracts in proteins may carry out a nutrient-sensing function by changing the protein level in response to extracellular amino acid availability.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the collective observations about polyQ protein sensitivity to amino acid availability.

claim: Amino acid depletion is associated with the loss of translational fidelity among polyglutamine-containing transcripts, which takes place in discrete areas of solid tumors in vivo.
source: Finally, our work demonstrates that amino acid depletion is associated with the loss of translational fidelity among polyglutamine-containing transcripts, which, as we demonstrate, takes place in discrete areas of solid tumors in vivo.
evidence: Supported by frameshift reporter data in vitro and xenograft immunohistochemistry data in vivo.
